summary: Describes a new End-to-End protocol between a host and its packet switch node (PSN, also called an IMP) on the ARPANET and MILNET. It is an updated version of a BBN report and aims to fix deficiencies in the old protocol, improve performance and throughput, and better support the growing number of hosts. Anyone supporting a host on those networks was urged to review it.

eli5.summary: Computers on an old network talked to the network's post office using a certain routine. This memo rewrites that routine so letters move faster and fewer get lost.

subtitle: Revised protocol for connecting hosts to the ARPANET and MILNET packet switch nodes.

tldr.problem: The ARPANET's original host-to-packet-switch protocol, designed in the early 1970s, was outdated. Networks had grown, new host protocols like X.25 and TCP/IP had replaced the old NCP, and the system needed better performance, flexibility, and reliability.
tldr.mechanism: The new End-to-End module uses source buffering with retransmission instead of destination buffering, supports multiple independent connections between hosts with configurable window sizes up to 127, and provides four precedence levels and hunt groups for addressing.
tldr.outcome: The revised protocol improves throughput by at least 50% for X.25 traffic, supports 500+ simultaneous connections per packet switch node, and allows the ARPANET to better serve its growing and changing host population.

today: RFC 979 describes the PSN End-to-End protocol implementation for the ARPANET and MILNET. The protocol has not been obsoleted. PSNs remain critical infrastructure for these networks.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 979 describes the new End-to-End (EE) protocol for the Packet Switch Nodes (PSNs), which are the routing computers (previously called IMPs) on the ARPANET and MILNET. The EE protocol handles the connection between a host computer and the packet switch node, and manages reliable delivery of data across the network.

The new EE is being deployed in PSN Release 7.0 alongside the old EE, with the network operations center able to switch individual PSNs or the entire network between them. Both versions are functionally equivalent when running the old EE, but they are incompatible when mixed.
sections.eli5: Computers on the ARPANET talk to a main post office computer called a Packet Switch Node. This RFC describes a new version of how that conversation works.

sections.title: Why a New Protocol Was Needed
sections.content:
The old EE was designed almost a decade earlier, in the early days of packet switching technology. The network environment had changed dramatically. Originally, only the ARPANET Host-IMP Protocol (AHIP) existed with the old NCP protocol above it. By 1986, X.25 was rapidly increasing and TCP/IP had replaced NCP.

The old EE had several limitations: it used a fixed window of only eight outstanding messages between any pair of hosts, relied on destination buffer preallocation rather than source retransmission, and did not support multiple independent connections between the same hosts. These constraints severely limited throughput, especially for networks with satellite links (which have long delays) and for gateways connecting multiple users' traffic.
sections.eli5: Networks had changed a lot since the old protocol was designed. The old way could only send eight messages at a time, and it was bad at recovering when messages got lost.

sections.title: Key Architectural Changes
sections.content:
The new EE introduces several major improvements. Full-duplex connections replace the old simplex connections, so two-way traffic like TCP no longer needs two separate connections. The EE can now open a connection and send a full message of data in the opening request itself, rather than requiring a separate opening sequence in each direction.

Source buffering with message retransmission replaces destination buffer preallocation, allowing the network to automatically recover from lost packets in the subnet without manual intervention. Adjustable windows replace the fixed eight-message limit, supporting up to 127 messages per connection and allowing up to 256 simultaneous independent connections between any pair of hosts.

The new EE supports four precedence levels and hunt groups for addressing, where multiple host ports on a destination PSN can share the same group identifier and incoming connections are evenly distributed across the group.
sections.eli5: The new protocol lets computers send messages in both directions at once, can keep many messages in flight at the same time, remembers messages in case they get lost, and lets groups of computers share one address.

sections.title: Network Services and Interoperability
sections.content:
The new EE provides unified network layer services for three types of host interfaces: X.25, the ARPANET Host-IMP Protocol (AHIP), and an interoperable service that allows X.25 and AHIP hosts to communicate with each other despite their different protocols.

All data packets and call requests are now source-buffered in the source PSN, providing reliable delivery that automatically recovers from lost packets in the subnet. The new EE supports end-to-end checksum for optional 32-bit data integrity checking across the entire network. Access control is expanded to allow 32 communities of interest (instead of 15), and the EE can enforce connection block preemption to reserve resources for higher-precedence connections when necessary.

The RFC defines DDN Standard Service Version 2 for interoperability between X.25 and AHIP hosts, improving upon Version 1 with better performance, direct mapping of precedence levels, support for up to 256 simultaneous connections, and end-to-end significance for acknowledgments.
sections.eli5: The new system can handle three different ways computers talk to it, and it even lets two computers that speak different languages understand each other. It keeps messages safe if they get lost and protects important traffic during congestion.

sections.title: Protocol Mechanisms and Performance
sections.content:
The EE peer protocol between packet switch nodes supports Internal ACKs (IACKs) and External ACKs (EACKs), both of which are piggybacked on reverse traffic when possible. IACKs cancel the retransmission timer and free source buffering when a message is completely reassembled, allowing the EE to avoid unnecessary retransmissions. EACKs advance the end-to-end window when the destination host acknowledges the message.

The ACK aggregation timer interacts carefully with the retransmission timer: when multiple IACKs and EACKs are combined, they can be sent back to the source PSN in fewer packets, or even piggybacked entirely on data traveling in the reverse direction. In the best case with bidirectional traffic, no additional network packets beyond the data messages are needed for acknowledgments.

Performance goals for the new EE include at least 50% improvement in X.25 throughput, support for at least 500 simultaneous connections per PSN and 50% more call setups per second, at least 400 packet buffers for source buffering and reassembly, support for at least 255 hosts per PSN and 1023 PSNs per network, and support for four message precedence levels with a maximum message length of 1024 bytes.
sections.eli5: The new protocol sends acknowledgments smartly, combining them together and attaching them to messages going the other way. It can handle many simultaneous conversations and prioritize important messages.
